connection_type: I have direct personal experience (as an immigrant, refugee, religious minority, or member of a marginalised group)
disclosure_text: As being the son to a immigrant, and second generation immigrant, I relate heavily to those topics since they directly impacted me my whole life and still to this day, it's not uncommon for me hear or see news or topics surrounding my situation.
micronarrative: I am drawn to the student whose reflection on marginalization gets lost in the sea of opinions. It feels like no matter how sensitive or important the topic, people are easily disregarded, and those dominating the conversation are always the loudest, not the ones that are more right. Growing up, I saw news pieces that villainized or lied about my experiences; because they were sensational and viral, they drove public attention no matter how wrong they were. I learned to blend in and listen more than speak, as it wasn’t worth arguing against firm beliefs on immigration or advantages since most of the people arguing had no true understanding of the root of the problem. This made me observative since instead of weakening my voice, hearing opposing viewpoints strengthened it. I became empathetic to those who are marginalized or quiet in public space, realizing early that media is not always right and forming my own opinions.

chat_log.content: Reading through that passage — what stands out to you first? Is there a moment, a feeling, or a person in it you find yourself drawn to?

In way yes, since growing I always read and saw things that villainizes or completely lie about my own experiences  marginalization, but since those news pieces were more sensational and more viral it drove public attention no matter how wrong it is.

I just learned to blend in, due to my own experiences, I got more empathetic to those that are marginalized or those are "quiet" in the public space. Another important thing I realized from a young age, is that media is sensationalized and not always right and to form my own opinions about things.
What specific cultural norms or expectations in your community required you to "blend in" rather than speak your truth?

While I wouldn't be for it or talk against what I personally believe, I  just learned to listened more than to speak because sometimes it was just wasn't worth it to ague against someone with very firm beliefs about immigration or how marginalized get more advantages despite not understanding the very root of it.

In a way it made more observative, and since I only listened most of the time, I learned why they got to those opinions and just how powerful media and news actually is. Instead of weakening my own voice, I feel like in way strengthen it since I heard and acknowledged the opposing viewpoints a lot.
